client: I got laid off from my job at the marketing firm about a month ago, and ever since then I've just been feeling completely overwhelmed by everything. The financial uncertainty is really getting to me — I keep running these worst-case scenarios in my head about money running out, and I can't seem to stop. Honestly, I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change anything, but I figured I'd give this a shot.
therapist: It takes real courage to reach out even when part of you isn't sure it will help — I'm glad you gave it a shot. Losing a job can shake so many things at once, and that loop of worst-case financial scenarios sounds genuinely exhausting to carry around. I'm curious — when those worst-case thoughts show up, what does the story your mind tells you usually look like at its darkest point?

client: At its darkest, my mind basically tells me I'm going to drain my savings completely, end up unable to pay rent, and just... lose everything I've worked for. Like, I'll picture myself having to call my parents for money at 34, which feels humiliating, or just being stuck in this downward spiral with no way out. It's like my brain won't let me consider any other outcome — it just keeps replaying that one terrible version of events over and over.
therapist: That image your mind keeps replaying — losing everything, having to call your parents — sounds really painful and heavy to sit with, especially when it feels like the only possible outcome. What you're describing is something we call "tunnel vision" in CBT, where our brain gets so locked onto the threat that it genuinely blocks out other possibilities, not because they don't exist, but because fear is a very loud narrator. I'd love to gently explore with you — when you look at where you actually stand right now, one month in, what's the real evidence that this worst-case ending is the *most likely* path, versus one of many possible ones?

client: I mean, objectively I know I still have some savings — probably enough for three or four months if I'm careful — and I've been applying to jobs and had a couple of responses already. But here's the thing, knowing that doesn't actually make the fear go away, so I'm not sure how useful it is to just list out the facts. It's like my brain hears the evidence and then immediately says "yeah, but what if that's not enough?"
therapist: You've actually just identified something really important — your brain is doing a classic move called "yes, but..." where it acknowledges the evidence and then immediately discounts it, which is why facts alone don't quiet the fear. You're right that listing evidence isn't enough on its own; the goal in CBT isn't just to *know* the safer thought, but to gradually help your nervous system *feel* it too, and that takes a bit more than logic. What do you notice happens in your body or your thinking right before the "yeah, but what if" kicks in — is there a particular moment or trigger that seems to set it off?

client: Honestly, it tends to happen most when I'm just sitting quietly — like at night when I'm trying to fall asleep, or in the morning before I've got anything to distract me. It's almost like the moment there's silence, my brain just rushes in to fill it with all this catastrophic stuff. I guess my body gets this tight, restless feeling in my chest, like I need to do something but there's nothing I can actually do right then.
therapist: That tight, restless feeling in your chest in those quiet moments makes a lot of sense — your nervous system is essentially trying to "solve" a problem at the exact time when you have the least ability to act on it, which creates this really uncomfortable loop. Those in-between moments — falling asleep, waking up — are actually when our brain's threat-detection system tends to be loudest, precisely because there's no task to anchor it. I'm wondering, when that chest tightness shows up, have you ever tried giving your brain a small, concrete "job" to do in that moment — something that gently interrupts the spiral before it picks up speed?

client: I've tried things like scrolling on my phone or putting on a show, but honestly that just feels like avoidance and it doesn't really help me sleep. I'm a little skeptical about the idea of giving my brain a "job" — like, what kind of job is actually going to compete with "you might lose your apartment"? It feels like bringing a flashlight to fight a wildfire.
therapist: I love that image — a flashlight against a wildfire — and I think your skepticism is actually really healthy and worth taking seriously rather than dismissing. The goal isn't to overpower the fear with a distraction, but more to gently shift your brain from "threat-scanning mode" into something slightly more grounded — things like slow breathing or a body scan work not because they're louder than the fear, but because they operate on a different channel entirely, speaking directly to your nervous system rather than trying to out-argue it. It's less about winning a debate with the wildfire and more about stepping out of the wind for a moment — does that distinction feel like it changes things at all, or does it still feel like too small a tool for what you're facing?

client: That framing actually does make a little more sense to me — like, I'm not trying to logic my way out of a panic, I'm just trying to change the physical state I'm in. But I guess my worry is that in that moment, when the spiral is already going, I won't even remember to try it, or I'll try it and it'll feel so mechanical that I'll just dismiss it. It's hard to practice something calmly when the whole problem is that I can't be calm.
therapist: You're raising something really practical and honest — it's genuinely hard to access a tool in the middle of a storm that you've only ever seen described on a calm day. That's actually why in CBT we try to build these practices *before* the spiral peaks, not as a rescue technique but as something familiar enough that it becomes almost automatic — like how you don't have to think about braking when a car stops suddenly, because your body already knows. What if we thought about finding one small, low-stakes moment in your day — not a crisis moment — where you could just experiment with it once, almost like a trial run with no pressure attached?

client: I guess that makes sense — like, building the muscle before I need it rather than trying to lift something heavy the first time. Maybe I could try it in the afternoon when I'm just sitting with coffee or something, when things aren't already spiraling. I'm still a little unsure it'll feel like anything other than just breathing, but I suppose trying it once when I'm not panicking doesn't cost me much.
therapist: That coffee moment sounds like a genuinely perfect starting point — low stakes, already a quiet pause in your day, and you've already claimed it as yours. And I'd actually encourage you to hold onto that "it'll probably just feel like breathing" expectation, because the first few times it *will* feel ordinary, and that's completely fine — you're not looking for a dramatic shift, just building a little familiarity with the tool. How will you know, even in a small way, if the experiment was worth repeating?

client: I think if I felt even slightly less tense during that afternoon moment — like even a small reduction in that chest tightness — that would probably be enough to make me try it again. But I'm also wondering if I'll just end up using that quiet time to check job listings or my bank account instead, because that feels more "productive" even though I know it probably makes things worse. I guess the honest answer is I'm not sure I'll actually prioritize it over the anxiety-driven stuff that feels more urgent.
therapist: You're being really honest with yourself there — recognizing that checking job listings or your bank account *feels* productive but probably feeds the anxiety rather than calming it is actually a meaningful insight, not a small one. That pull toward urgency is so understandable, but what you're describing is essentially choosing the thing that keeps the alarm bell ringing because silence feels riskier than noise. I'm curious — if you imagine both versions of that afternoon moment side by side, the bank-checking one and the breathing one, what do you think each version of you feels like an hour later?

client: Honestly, when I picture the bank-checking version, I know that an hour later I'd probably feel more wound up — like I'd have just given myself more ammunition for the spiral. The breathing version is harder to picture clearly, but I suppose the most realistic outcome is just... feeling neutral, maybe a little less tense, which isn't exciting but is probably better than worse. I think part of why I resist it is that "neutral" doesn't feel like enough when everything feels so urgent, even though I can see logically that neutral is actually a step in the right direction right now.
therapist: What you just said is genuinely insightful — that "neutral" feels disappointing when urgency is screaming for a dramatic solution, even though neutral *is* actually progress when your baseline has been so activated. There's something worth sitting with there: in the middle of a crisis, calm doesn't feel like winning, but it's actually the foundation everything else gets built on. I wonder if it might help to quietly reframe that afternoon experiment not as "trying to feel better" but as "practicing not making things worse" — does that feel like a more honest and achievable goal for where you are right now?

client: Yeah, "practicing not making things worse" actually lands differently than "trying to feel better" — it feels more honest about where I am, less like I'm setting myself up to fail some invisible test. I think I've been putting so much pressure on every small thing to fix the big problem that even a breathing exercise starts to feel like it has to justify itself. That framing takes some of that weight off, so I think I can actually commit to trying it during that coffee moment this week.
therapist: It sounds like something genuinely shifted just now — a little quieter, a little less pressured — and I want to acknowledge that, because reframing how you measure progress is actually real cognitive work, not just a small tweak. You've gone from "this has to fix everything" to "I'm just practicing not making things worse," and that's a more sustainable and honest relationship with the process. As you head into this week, I'm curious — is there anything you think might get in the way of that coffee moment, that we could think through now so it doesn't catch you off guard?
